text: You've now seen three pieces of the error mitigation picture separately: noise models that simulate imperfection, readout correction that undoes measurement bias, and zero-noise extrapolation that estimates an unreachable ideal value. This lab puts them to work together.

Recall the noisy measurement from the noise-models lesson: a qubit prepared in |0>, with a 2% bit-flip error injected right before measurement, gave a result of roughly 1000 and 24 out of 1024 shots. Here's the question worth sitting with: if you only had those counts in front of you, could you tell that error came from a gate rather than from the measurement hardware itself misreporting a perfectly prepared |0>? For a single qubit measured once per shot, the answer is no — a gate error right before measurement and a pure readout error produce statistically indistinguishable counts. Distinguishing them requires a separate characterization experiment that isolates the measurement step from the rest of the circuit.

Take the calibration matrix from the readout-mitigation lesson and pick a fresh observed vector of your own, say 0.60 and 0.40. Multiplying by the inverse matrix gives back corrected values. Confirm two things: the corrected values still sum to 1, as any valid probability distribution must, and the correction shifts your numbers in a sensible direction relative to what the calibration matrix says about the device's bias.

From the ZNE lesson, walk through the same computation using lambda 1 and lambda 3 instead of lambda 1 and lambda 2. Three times E of 1 minus E of 3, divided by 2, works out to the same 0.80 — a different pair of points, the same answer, exactly what you'd expect from data that's exactly linear by construction.

Step back and notice what each technique actually did. Readout correction didn't make the hardware stop misreporting outcomes — it used a known bias pattern to recover a better estimate from biased data, a recovery that degrades once real shot noise is layered on top. ZNE didn't make the real circuit run with less noise — it ran at more noise, deliberately, and used the resulting trend to estimate a point it never actually touched. In both cases, you're squeezing a better answer out of multiple imperfect measurements after the fact — the underlying hardware noise is still there on every real run.
Chapter 8 closes out the course with a capstone: building a real circuit simulator project from everything you've learned, starting with defining exactly what it needs to do.
